notes: Ruling slot 1 = Independence Party (Bjarni Benediktsson). The real coalition partner of the Viðreisn government is the Social Democratic Party, placed by ideology in slot 3; template coalition slot 2 holds the Union of Liberals and Leftists (founded Nov 1969). Progressive Party moved from MD slot 15 to slot 14 (has starting popularity; keeps its MD sprite). People's Alliance in slot 4 (communist core, popularity) rather than 18. Islamic slots use real transnational institutions, as Iceland has virtually no Muslims.

0.name: Samtök um vestræna samvinnu
0.text:
The Association for Western Cooperation was founded in 1958 by supporters of the three pro-NATO parties – the Independence Party, the Progressive Party and the Social Democrats – to defend Iceland's membership of the Atlantic Alliance and the American-manned Iceland Defence Force at Keflavík. Its youth counterpart, Varðberg, carries the same message to students and young professionals.

The association holds that a small, unarmed island in the middle of the North Atlantic can only be safe under the NATO umbrella, and that the growing presence of the Soviet fleet makes the base indispensable. It organises lectures, publications and study trips to NATO headquarters. Its leverage lies in the leaderships of the governing parties, the foreign ministry and the press, above all Morgunblaðið.

1.name: Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn
1.text:
The Independence Party, founded in 1929 by the merger of the Conservative and Liberal parties, is Iceland's largest political force, with 37.5 percent of the vote in the 1967 election. Its chairman Bjarni Benediktsson has been Prime Minister since 1963, heading the Viðreisn coalition with the Social Democrats that has governed since 1959; Jóhann Hafstein is his deputy and Geir Hallgrímsson Mayor of Reykjavík.

The party stands for free enterprise, a liberalised economy, firm membership of NATO and the American base at Keflavík. Having steered Iceland through the herring collapse of 1967–68 with two devaluations, it has just negotiated entry into EFTA. Its base spans business, the professions, much of the fishing industry and many urban workers, and the daily Morgunblaðið is its voice.

2.name: Samtök frjálslyndra og vinstri manna
2.text:
The Union of Liberals and Leftists was founded in November 1969 by Hannibal Valdimarsson, the veteran president of the Icelandic Confederation of Labour, and Björn Jónsson, after they broke with the People's Alliance over the dominance of its old communist core. It gathers left-wing social democrats, former members of the neutralist National Preservation Party and radical liberals impatient with all the established parties.

The Union wants a broad, non-communist left, a fairer distribution of the gains of growth, a stronger regional policy and the extension of Iceland's fishing limits. It is sceptical of the American base and would like to see it phased out. Its strength lies in Hannibal's personal following in the Westfjords and the trade unions, and in its appeal to voters seeking a fresh start.

3.name: Alþýðuflokkurinn
3.text:
The Social Democratic Party, founded in 1916 together with the Icelandic Confederation of Labour, is the junior partner in the Viðreisn government. Its chairman, Gylfi Þ. Gíslason, is Minister of Education and Commerce, and its former leader Emil Jónsson is Foreign Minister. The party took 15.7 percent of the vote in 1967 and has governed alongside the Independence Party for more than a decade.

The party is moderate, reformist and firmly Western, supporting NATO membership, EFTA entry and the modernisation of the economy, while defending the welfare system it helped build: social insurance, workers' housing and public pensions. Its base lies among organised workers, seamen and civil servants in Reykjavík and Hafnarfjörður, but it competes for the labour vote with the socialists and Hannibal's new movement.

4.name: Alþýðubandalagið
4.text:
The People's Alliance began in 1956 as an electoral alliance between the Socialist Party and Hannibal Valdimarsson's left social democrats and became a formal party in November 1968, when the Socialist Party dissolved itself into it. Its chairman is Ragnar Arnalds, while Lúðvík Jósepsson leads it in the Althing and Magnús Kjartansson edits its daily Þjóðviljinn. Together with Hannibal's list it won 17.6 percent in 1967.

The Alliance is socialist and fiercely nationalist, demanding withdrawal from NATO, the closure of the American base and a unilateral extension of the fishing limits. Its old communist core keeps its ties with Moscow, although the party condemned the invasion of Czechoslovakia. Its base lies in the trade unions, the fishing towns and among writers and intellectuals.

5.name: Æskulýðsfylkingin
5.text:
The Youth Front, known simply as Fylkingin, began in 1938 as the youth league of the Socialist Party but has broken away from the People's Alliance to become the home of Iceland's New Left. It made its name leading the stormy protests against the NATO ministerial meeting in Reykjavík in June 1968 and the demonstrations against the Vietnam War outside the American embassy.

Fylkingin rejects parliamentary reformism and calls for revolutionary socialism, immediate withdrawal from NATO and solidarity with Vietnam and other liberation struggles. Trotskyist, Maoist and anarchist ideas compete within its small ranks of students and young workers. Its leverage lies in street mobilisation, its influence in the student movement and its talent for embarrassing the government.

6.name: Austurviðskiptin
6.text:
The Eastern Trade lobby is the network of fish exporters, herring salters and oil importers whose business rests on the barter trade with the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. Since the British ban on Icelandic fish landings in 1952, Moscow has bought frozen fillets and salted herring and paid largely in oil, which now covers most of Iceland's fuel needs.

Conservative businessmen rather than socialists, its members put markets before alliances. They resent Britain and West Germany over the fishing limits, warn that any quarrel with Moscow would cripple the economy, and urge governments to keep the Eastern contracts flowing whatever NATO thinks. Their leverage lies in the export sales organisations, the oil companies and the dependence of every fishing town on Soviet orders.

7.name: Menningartengsl Íslands og Ráðstjórnarríkjanna
7.text:
MÍR, the Iceland–USSR Cultural Society, was founded in 1950 to promote friendship with the Soviet Union and remains the meeting place of the pro-Moscow old guard of the dissolved Socialist Party. It organises film shows, exhibitions, language courses and delegations to the Soviet Union, working closely with the large Soviet embassy on Garðastræti in Reykjavík.

Its loyalists see the Soviet Union as the model of socialism and the natural friend of a small nation burdened with NATO bases, and they watch the People's Alliance's distancing from Moscow after the invasion of Czechoslovakia with dismay. Few in number and ageing, they matter through their contacts with Soviet diplomats and trade officials, their place in the trade-union old guard and their stubborn loyalty.

8.name: Islamisches Zentrum Hamburg
8.text:
The Islamic Centre Hamburg was established at the end of the 1950s by Iranian merchants in Hamburg with the support of Grand Ayatollah Borujerdi, and its Imam Ali Mosque on the Alster is the principal Shia centre of Northern Europe. Its director since 1965 is the cleric Mohammad Beheshti, who has made it a meeting point for Iranian students across West Germany and Scandinavia.

The centre preaches a modern, educated Shia Islam that engages with Western thought while asserting religion's role in public life. Beheshti encourages Islamic student associations and quietly maintains contacts with the clerical opposition to the Shah. In Iceland, which has almost no Muslims, its reach is limited to literature arriving through Scandinavian student circles and the occasional Iranian visitor.

9.name: Hizb al-Da'wa al-Islamiyya
9.text:
The Islamic Dawa Party is a clandestine Shia movement founded in Najaf in the late 1950s by young clerics and laymen around Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr. Since the Ba'athist government turned on the Najaf seminaries in 1969 its members are hunted in Iraq, and its ideas travel with Iraqi Shia students and doctors to the universities of Western Europe and Scandinavia.

Da'wa aims at an Islamic state guided by the Shia clergy and rejects both Western capitalism and Ba'athist or communist socialism, offering al-Sadr's Islamic economics as the alternative. Its cells are secretive and disciplined. Its reach to Iceland is limited to pamphlets passed between Muslim students in Copenhagen and Stockholm, but it offers a militant answer to both blocs.

10.name: Rabitat al-'Alam al-Islami
10.text:
The Muslim World League was founded in Mecca in 1962 under Saudi patronage to spread Islam and unite Muslims against secular nationalism and communism. Its secretary-general, Muhammad Surur al-Sabban, directs a growing network of missionaries, scholarships, publications and mosque-building grants financed by the Saudi kingdom's oil revenues.

The League promotes a conservative, Salafi-inclined Sunni Islam loyal to established rulers and to the House of Saud as guardian of the holy places. In Europe it supports mosques and Islamic centres from London to Copenhagen. For the handful of Muslims passing through Iceland – foreign students, seamen and diplomats – its Koran translations and literature are the main link to organised Islam.

11.name: Hizb ut-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Party of Liberation, was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani, who leads it from exile in Beirut. Banned across the Arab world, it organises in secret cells in Jordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon and among Arab students at universities in West Germany and Austria.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy and socialism as alien to Islam and works to restore the Caliphate by winning over army officers and intellectuals. Its members study al-Nabhani's writings and draft constitution in disciplined circles. With no base in Iceland, its message reaches the island only through the occasional Arab student or seaman, but it offers a total alternative to both Cold War blocs.

12.name: Centre Islamique de Genève
12.text:
The Islamic Centre of Geneva was founded in 1961 by Said Ramadan, son-in-law of the Muslim Brotherhood's founder Hasan al-Banna and the Brotherhood's leading figure in European exile. From Geneva it publishes, trains activists and links Muslim student associations across Western Europe, keeping ties with the Brotherhood's persecuted branches in Egypt and Syria.

The centre advocates an Islamic revival through education, preaching and organisation, aiming at societies governed by Islamic law without violent revolution. Anti-communist and hostile to the Arab nationalist regimes, it finds friends among conservative Gulf patrons. Iceland lies beyond its practical reach, but a few Muslim students at Nordic universities read its journals and keep in contact with its circles.

13.name: Seðlabanki Íslands
13.text:
The Central Bank of Iceland, established in 1961 out of the National Bank, is the technocratic heart of the Viðreisn economic policy. Its governor Jóhannes Nordal, an economist trained at the London School of Economics, works with the government's Economic Institute to manage the exchange rate, credit and the foreign borrowing behind projects such as the Búrfell power station and the Straumsvík aluminium smelter.

The bank's experts believe a small, fish-dependent economy needs firm, depoliticised management: realistic exchange rates, curbs on inflation, liberalised trade and foreign capital for industrialisation. They engineered the devaluations of 1967 and 1968 after the herring collapse and back entry into EFTA. Their leverage lies in expertise, control of credit and the confidence of foreign lenders.

14.name: Framsóknarflokkurinn
14.text:
The Progressive Party, founded in 1916 as the party of farmers and the cooperative movement, is Iceland's second-largest party and has led the opposition since 1959. Its chairman Ólafur Jóhannesson, a professor of law, succeeded Eysteinn Jónsson in 1968, and the party took 28 percent of the vote in 1967. It is closely bound to the Federation of Icelandic Cooperative Societies, which dominates rural trade.

The party is agrarian and centrist, defending rural communities, regional development and farm support against the Reykjavík-centred liberalism of the government. It is pragmatic on NATO but increasingly open to closing the American base, and it backs a rapid extension of the fishing limits. Its strongholds are the countryside and the coastal towns of the north and east.

15.name: Landssamband íslenskra útvegsmanna
15.english: Federation of Icelandic Fishing Vessel Owners
15.text:
The Federation of Icelandic Fishing Vessel Owners, founded in 1939, unites the owners of the trawlers and motor boats on which the national economy rests: fish make up some nine-tenths of Iceland's exports. Its members range from municipal trawler companies to the private fishing firms and family dynasties of Reykjavík, Hafnarfjörður, the Westmann Islands and the Westfjords.

The federation lobbies relentlessly on the exchange rate, fuel prices, fishing loans and the fish prices set by the price board, and it was the loudest voice demanding devaluation after the herring catch collapsed in 1967–68. It favours wider fishing limits and close ties with the governing parties. Its leverage is enormous: when the boats stay in harbour, the whole country stops.

16.name: Verzlunarráð Íslands
16.text:
The Iceland Chamber of Commerce, founded in 1917, represents the country's merchants, wholesalers, importers and a growing number of industrial firms. Close to the Independence Party, it has been the chief business ally of the Viðreisn government's liberalisation since 1960, when import licensing and multiple exchange rates were largely swept away.

The chamber stands for free enterprise, free trade and a smaller state, campaigning against price controls, high taxes, the privileges of the cooperative movement and the political allocation of bank credit. It welcomes EFTA membership and foreign investment as the way to diversify an economy hostage to fish. Its leverage lies in its members' place in trade and credit and in its ties to the governing party.

17.name: Landvernd
17.text:
The Icelandic Environment Association, Landvernd, was founded on 25 October 1969 by a broad coalition of associations, from farmers' and women's societies to youth groups, to fight the soil erosion and land degradation that have stripped much of Iceland of its vegetation since the settlement. It is the country's first national umbrella body for conservation.

Landvernd campaigns for land reclamation, controls on overgrazing, the protection of natural sites and a public voice in decisions on hydropower and industry. Its founding coincides with mounting conflict over plans to dam the Laxá river below Lake Mývatn, which local farmers fear will ruin a unique landscape. Its leverage lies in broad civic support, the backing of scientists and a growing national pride in nature.

18.name: Samtök hernámsandstæðinga
18.text:
The Organisation of Occupation Opponents was founded at Þingvellir in 1960 to campaign against the American military presence its members call an occupation. Its yearly march from the Keflavík base to Reykjavík has become a ritual of the Icelandic left, drawing socialists, nationalists, writers, students and not a few members of the Progressive Party.

The movement demands the departure of the American forces, withdrawal from NATO and a return to the permanent neutrality proclaimed in 1918. It sees the base as a threat to Icelandic culture as much as to security and has campaigned against the base's television broadcasts. It gives Icelandic neutralism a broad, popular face, and its leverage is felt whenever the base question returns to the agenda.

19.name: Rauða kverið
19.text:
The Little Red Book circles are small groups of Maoist students in Reykjavík and among Icelanders studying in Scandinavia, who read Chairman Mao's quotations, celebrate the Cultural Revolution and have begun to break away from both the People's Alliance and Fylkingin.

They denounce the Soviet Union as a 'social-imperialist' superpower no better than the United States, condemn the People's Alliance as revisionist, and call for a genuine Marxist-Leninist party rooted in the working class, solidarity with Vietnam and Albania, and the expulsion of both superpowers from the North Atlantic. Their numbers are tiny and their meetings fractious, but their zeal finds an echo in the radicalised student movement.

20.name: Stéttarsamband bænda
20.text:
The Farmers' Association of Iceland, founded in 1945, is the farmers' own union, negotiating each year with consumer representatives over the prices that agricultural products may fetch. Its chairman since 1963 is Gunnar Guðbjartsson, and it works hand in hand with the Agricultural Society and the cooperative movement.

The association speaks for a countryside that feels abandoned as young people leave for Reykjavík and the government courts foreign capital, aluminium smelters and free trade. It defends price guarantees, export subsidies for lamb and dairy, rural credit and the dignity of the farming way of life against urban critics who call it a burden. Its leverage lies in the overweighting of rural votes in the Althing and its bond with the Progressive Party.

21.name: Þjóðernissinnar
21.text:
The Nationalists are a scattering of ageing veterans and young admirers of the Icelandic Nationalist Movement of the 1930s, which marched under the swastika before fading away during the war. Without a party, newspaper or public leader, they meet in private and circulate translated German and Scandinavian far-right literature.

They preach racial nationalism, the defence of Icelandic blood and culture against foreign influence, and an authoritarian state above party quarrels, mixing hatred of communism with resentment of the American presence and the Americanisation of youth. Their influence is negligible, but they feed on anger over the base, the cultural upheaval of the 1960s and a sense that the old Iceland is vanishing.

22.name: Landhelgisgæsla Íslands
22.text:
The Icelandic Coast Guard is the only armed service of a country without an army. Under its director Pétur Sigurðsson, in charge since 1952, its handful of patrol vessels and aircraft police the twelve-mile fishing limit won in the first Cod War against Britain in 1958–61 and provide rescue at sea in some of the world's most dangerous waters.

The Coast Guard embodies the nation's struggle for its fishing grounds, and its captains are national heroes. It stands ready to enforce any further extension of the limits against British and West German trawlers. Professional and apolitical, it has no ambitions of its own, but as the sole armed force of a nation without soldiers its loyalty and morale matter to any government.

23.name: Huset Glücksborg
23.text:
The House of Glücksburg, Denmark's royal dynasty, reigned over Iceland until 1944: Christian X was King of Iceland after the Act of Union of 1918 made the island a sovereign kingdom in personal union with Denmark. The Althing proclaimed the republic at Þingvellir on 17 June 1944 while Denmark was under German occupation. Christian's son, King Frederick IX, has reigned in Copenhagen since 1947.

There is no organised monarchist movement in Iceland, but a few older conservatives still regret the manner of the break with the crown and admire the stability of the Nordic monarchies, seeing a king as a symbol above party strife. Their leverage is purely sentimental, nourished by history and by the warm reconciliation embodied in Denmark's agreement to return the medieval manuscripts.
